sense: how well someone or something does

terms.gloss: do (well or badly) at something, manage
terms.grammar: phrase: gerō with rem and an adverb (bene, male, fēlīciter)
evidence: Ennius in Cic. Fam. 7.6.1: multī suam rem bene gessēre
Cic. Sen. 22: male rem gerentibus patribus
terms.comment: Latin has no noun for how well someone does; it says how they managed, with an adverb: bene rem gessit, he did well; male rem gerere, to make a poor job of one’s affairs (Cic. Sen. 22). Lewis & Short gives rem gerere of public business and, in Plautus and Cicero, of private affairs.

terms.gloss: acquit oneself, perform (in a role or an office)
terms.grammar: phrase: gerō with the reflexive and an adverb or a clause of manner
evidence: Cic. Leg. agr. 1.26: sīc mē in hōc magistrātū geram
terms.comment: The same phrase is used of behaviour (see behaviour).

terms.gloss: how did you get on? what came of it?
evidence: Ter. Ph. 682: Quid ēgistī? — Ēmūnxī argentō senēs.
terms.comment: Asks what someone has got done, or how a thing they went off to do turned out.

phrases.latin: Multī suam rem bene gessēre et pūblicam patriā procul; multī, quī domī aetātem agerent, proptereā sunt improbātī.
phrases.english: Many have done well for themselves and for the state far from home; many who spent their lives at home have been thought the less of for it.

phrases.latin: Sīc mē in hōc magistrātū geram, patrēs cōnscrīptī, ut possim tribūnum plēbis reī pūblicae īrātum coercēre, mihi īrātum contemnere.
phrases.english: I shall so acquit myself in this office, senators, that I can restrain a tribune who is angry with the state and disregard one who is angry with me.
How did you get on? — I’ve cleaned the old men out of their money.
